headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Post-Natal Care
headings.content: Post-natal care (PNC), often referred to as postpartum care, is a critical phase in maternal and child health that begins immediately after the birth of the placenta and extends up to the first six weeks (42 days) of life. For nursing students in Nigeria preparing for clinical practice and professional examinations, understanding PNC is vital because this period carries a high risk for maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Post-natal care encompasses the systematic monitoring, assessment, and support of the mother and her newborn to ensure physical recovery, emotional well-being, and successful adaptation to parenting. During this transitional period, physiological restoration occurs alongside psychological adjustments, such as bonding and the prevention of postpartum mood disorders. The World Health Organization and the Nigerian Federal Ministry of Health emphasize that PNC is not a single event but a continuum of care starting right from the delivery room. Nurses play a frontline role in delivering this care by providing compassionate, evidence-based interventions tailored to the socio-cultural realities of Nigerian communities. Effective post-natal care helps bridge the gap between hospital delivery and home life, ensuring early detection of life-threatening complications such as postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis, and neonatal jaundice. By fostering an environment of continuous health education, nurses empower mothers to recognize danger signs and seek timely medical intervention, thereby significantly contributing to the reduction of maternal and child mortality ratios across Nigeria.

headings.title: Objectives and Timing of Post-Natal Visits
headings.content: The primary objectives of post-natal visits are to promote the health and recovery of both mother and newborn, facilitate bonding, encourage exclusive breastfeeding, provide family planning counseling, and detect and manage any deviations from normal recovery early. To achieve these goals, a structured schedule of post-natal visits is essential according to global and national guidelines. The first contact should occur within 24 hours of birth, ideally within the first hour if the delivery took place in a health facility. If the mother delivered at home, a skilled birth attendant or community health nurse should visit within 24 hours. Subsequent routine visits are scheduled at specific intervals: the second visit takes place on day 3 (between 48 to 72 hours), the third visit between days 7 and 14, and a final comprehensive post-natal check-up at six weeks postpartum. Each visit serves a specific purpose. Early visits focus heavily on immediate postpartum hemorrhage detection, perineal wound checks, initiation of breastfeeding, and assessing the baby's thermal regulation and feeding efficacy. Mid-term visits monitor ongoing involution, umbilical cord healing, and maternal emotional status, screening specifically for postpartum blues or depression. The six-week visit marks the physiological conclusion of the puerperium, allowing the nurse to evaluate long-term recovery, provide definitive family planning options, perform cervical screening if indicated, and ensure complete immunization updates for the infant. Adhering to this timetable ensures that no mother or baby falls through the cracks of the healthcare system.

headings.title: Physiological Changes and Puerperium Involution
headings.content: The puerperium is the period following childbirth during which the body's anatomical and physiological changes revert back to their non-pregnant state, typically lasting about six weeks. A central concept in this phase is involution, which refers primarily to the rapid reduction in the size of the uterus. Immediately following delivery, the fundus is palpable about midway between the symphysis pubis and the umbilicus. Within 24 hours, it rises to the level of the umbilicus and thereafter decreases by approximately one centimeter (one finger-breadth) every day, becoming a pelvic organ again by the tenth to twelfth day and returning to its pre-pregnant size by six weeks. Nurses must monitor fundal height, consistency (firm versus boggy), and tenderness regularly. Subinvolution, the failure of the uterus to return to its normal size, can lead to postpartum hemorrhage and requires prompt nursing intervention. Alongside uterine involution is the discharge of lochia, the intrauterine waste consisting of blood, tissue, and mucus. Lochia progresses through three stages: lochia rubra (red, lasting days 1 to 3), lochia serosa (pinkish-brown, lasting days 4 to 10), and lochia alba (whitish-yellow, lasting up to three weeks or more). Cervical changes also occur, with the external os closing slowly and permanently changing from a round dimple to a transverse slit. Hormonal shifts involve a dramatic drop in estrogen and progesterone, which triggers lactation and metabolic resets. Understanding these physiological milestones enables the nurse to differentiate normal recovery processes from pathological conditions such as retained placental fragments or uterine infection.

headings.title: Comprehensive Post-Natal Maternal Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive post-natal maternal assessment requires a holistic, systematic approach combining physical examination, psychological evaluation, and social screening. The nurse begins by reviewing the birth history, noting any complications like prolonged labor, instrument delivery, or postpartum hemorrhage. Physical assessment starts with vital signs: blood pressure is monitored closely to detect postpartum pre-eclampsia or hypotension from blood loss; temperature is assessed to rule out puerperal sepsis; and pulse rate is checked for tachycardia. Head-to-toe examination includes checking the conjunctiva for pallor (indicating anemia, a common issue among Nigerian women), inspecting the breasts for engorgement, nipple integrity, and milk production, and palpating the abdomen to assess uterine involution and bladder distension. Perineal assessment is crucial, especially for mothers who had episiotomies or spontaneous lacerations; the nurse inspects the wound using the REEDA scale (Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation) to ensure proper healing and rule out hematoma or infection. Lower extremities must be examined for signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), such as unilateral swelling, warmth, and calf tenderness, which can be exacerbated by immobility. Psychologically, the nurse evaluates the mother's mood, emotional attachment to the newborn, and support systems, remaining vigilant for signs of postpartum blues, depression, or psychosis. Documenting these findings accurately allows the interprofessional healthcare team to intervene swiftly and support a safe recovery.

headings.title: Newborn Assessment and Routine Care
headings.content: Newborn assessment and routine care form a cornerstone of post-natal nursing duties, ensuring that the neonate transitions successfully from intrauterine to extrauterine life. Immediately after birth, the nurse performs an initial rapid assessment using the Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes to evaluate heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color. Routine immediate care involves drying the baby thoroughly to prevent hypothermia, clearing the airway if necessary, ensuring skin-to-skin contact, and initiating early breastfeeding within the first hour of life. Prophylactic interventions are then administered, including the application of tetracycline eye ointment to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum and an intramuscular injection of Vitamin K to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. A comprehensive physical examination of the newborn is conducted within 24 hours to detect any congenital anomalies or birth injuries. This includes measuring weight, length, and head circumference, listening to heart and lung sounds, palpating the abdomen and fontanelles, checking the patency of the anus, and inspecting the umbilical cord stump. The nurse also educates the mother on umbilical cord care, emphasizing dry cord care without applying harmful traditional substances like saliva, herbs, or toothpaste. Monitoring elimination patterns—ensuring the baby passes meconium within 24-48 hours and voids urine appropriately—provides critical reassurance regarding gastrointestinal and renal function.

headings.title: Identification and Management of Post-Partum Complications
headings.content: The identification and management of postpartum complications are critical competencies for nurses working in maternal-child health settings. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), defined as blood loss exceeding 500 mL following vaginal delivery or 1000 mL following a cesarean section, remains a leading cause of maternal mortality in Nigeria. The nurse must recognize the causes of PPH, commonly remembered through the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony, the most common cause), Tissue (retained placental fragments), Trauma (lacerations or uterine rupture), and Thrombin (coagulation disorders). Immediate nursing actions for PPH include calling for help, performing bimanual uterine massage, administering uterotonic drugs such as oxytocin, misoprostol, or ergometrine as prescribed, establishing large-bore intravenous access for fluid resuscitation, and monitoring vital signs. Another major complication is puerperal sepsis, an infection of the genital tract occurring at any time between rupture of membranes or labor and the 42nd day postpartum; signs include fever, foul-smelling lochia, and lower abdominal pain. Nurses must monitor for thromboembolic events, postpartum hypertension disorders, and mastitis—an infection of the breast tissue characterized by localized pain, redness, and fever, often linked to milk stasis and cracked nipples. Prompt identification, advocacy for medical intervention, and meticulous supportive care can save a mother's life during these acute emergencies.

headings.title: Post-Natal Nutrition, Hygiene, and Self-Care
headings.content: Post-natal nutrition, personal hygiene, and self-care form the foundation of a mother's physical recovery and her ability to care for her newborn. Nutritional needs during the postnatal and lactation period are even higher than during pregnancy. Nursing education must emphasize a balanced diet rich in proteins, iron, calcium, and vitamins to replenish nutrient stores lost during childbirth and support breast milk production. In the Nigerian context, nurses should encourage the utilization of affordable, locally available food sources such as beans, lean meats, fish, eggs, dark green leafy vegetables, and whole grains, supplemented with routine micronutrients like iron and folate. Adequate fluid intake—primarily water—is essential, especially before and during breastfeeding sessions, to prevent dehydration and maintain milk volume. Regarding hygiene, nurses dispel harmful cultural myths that discourage bathing during the puerperium; regular bathing with clean water and soap is vital to prevent skin and perineal infections. Perineal hygiene involves washing the area from front to back after using the toilet and changing sanitary pads frequently to avoid bacterial proliferation. Rest and sleep hygiene are equally important, as fatigue can impair immune function and contribute to postpartum depression; nurses should counsel mothers to rest whenever the baby sleeps. Encouraging gentle postpartum exercises helps tone abdominal and pelvic floor muscles, promoting overall physical and mental well-being.

headings.title: Family Planning and Post-Partum Sexual Health
headings.content: Family planning and postpartum sexual health are essential components of comprehensive post-natal care that directly impact maternal and child spacing, health, and survival. Following childbirth, couples often have questions and concerns regarding the resumption of sexual intercourse and the risk of unintended pregnancy. Nurses must provide non-judgmental, comprehensive counseling tailored to the couple's reproductive goals and cultural beliefs. Physiologically, sexual intercourse can typically be resumed safely once the lochia has ceased, the perineal wound or episiotomy has completely healed, and the mother feels emotionally and physically ready, which often coincides with the six-week post-natal check-up. However, fertility can return before the first postpartum menstruation, making immediate contraceptive counseling vital during early post-natal visits. The nurse educates mothers on various family planning methods suitable for the postpartum period. For breastfeeding mothers, the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) is a highly effective, natural temporary method if specific criteria are met: the infant is exclusively breastfed, the mother is amenorrheic, and the baby is under six months of age. Other options include progestin-only contraceptives (such as pills, injectables like Depo-Provera, or implants), intrauterine devices (IUDs) inserted either immediately postpartum or at the six-week visit, barrier methods like condoms, and permanent methods like tubal ligation. By providing accurate information, nurses help women make informed choices, prevent closely spaced pregnancies, and safeguard their reproductive health.

headings.title: Community Integration and Primary Health Care Services for Mothers
headings.content: Community integration and primary health care (PHC) services for mothers bridge the gap between facility-based post-natal care and long-term family and community health. In Nigeria, primary health care centers serve as the grassroots level of healthcare delivery, making community integration vital for ensuring continuity of care after hospital discharge. Nurses play a pivotal role in linking postpartum mothers to community health extension workers (CHEWs), traditional birth attendants (TBAs) where appropriate, and community support groups. Effective community integration involves home visitation programs where community health nurses visit mother-infant dyads at home to assess living conditions, evaluate infant feeding practices, observe sibling dynamics, and reinforce danger sign education in a familiar environment. Furthermore, PHC services coordinate essential public health programs such as the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), ensuring that infants receive their BCG, oral polio, pentavalent, and pneumococcal vaccines on schedule. Community-based education also tackles socio-cultural barriers, gender dynamics, and myths surrounding postpartum practices by engaging community and religious leaders. Nurses advocate for male involvement in post-natal care, recognizing that supportive partners enhance maternal mental health, improve nutrition, and facilitate transport during obstetric emergencies. Strengthening community-PHC networks creates a resilient safety net that protects maternal and child health long after the initial postpartum period has ended.
